prompt: Why do fresh linking variables let a long CNF clause become a linear-size chain of three-literal clauses?

options.text: They force every original literal to be true
options.explanation: The original clause requires only one true literal.

options.text: They carry an unsatisfied clause forwards until some original literal satisfies it
options.explanation: The chain can be extended to a satisfying assignment exactly when at least one original literal is true.

options.text: They enumerate all assignments to the original variables
options.explanation: The construction is local and linear; it does not solve the formula.

options.text: They can be shared freely between unrelated clauses
options.explanation: Unrelated clauses need fresh variables to avoid introducing unwanted dependencies.

workedExample: The first split clause passes an unsatisfied choice into a fresh variable; each middle clause passes it onwards. If all original literals are false, the final clause fails. If some original literal is true, the fresh variables can be set to satisfy the chain. Only constant work is added per original literal, so the translation remains linear in clause length.

prompt:
Is this 2-SAT formula satisfiable?

```formula essential
F = (x ∨ y) ∧ (¬x ∨ y)
  ∧ (x ∨ ¬y) ∧ (¬x ∨ ¬y)
where
F: the whole formula
x, y: Boolean variables, each true or false
∨: OR: a clause is true when at least one side is true
∧: AND: all four clauses must be true
¬: NOT: ¬x is true exactly when x is false
In words: four two-literal clauses over x and y, all of which must hold.
```

Use the implication-graph method.

options.text: Yes, with x true and y true
options.explanation: This falsifies the last clause, (not x or not y).

options.text: Yes, with x true and y false
options.explanation: This falsifies the second clause, (not x or y).

options.text: No: x and ¬x end up in the same strongly connected component
options.explanation: Correct. The implication graph has a path from x through y to not-x, and a path from not-x through y back to x. So x and its negation reach each other, which means unsatisfiable.

options.text: It can't be decided efficiently, because SAT is NP-complete
options.explanation: 2-SAT is a special case that is in P. NP-completeness of general SAT says nothing about restricted versions.

workedExample: If the first variable is true, the second clause forces the second variable true and the fourth forces it false. If the first variable is false, the first clause forces the second variable true and the third forces it false. Thus either choice contradicts an implication. The first variable and its negation reach each other, so the formula is unsatisfiable.
